voice: Valory B – Conversational Girl-Next-Door with Relatable Vibe

lines.text: Here's a problem of the kind you'd actually be handed in an interview. And the code turns out to be the easy half.
You've been keeping a note of how many pages you read each day. The question is: on how many days did you beat your own average?
And your average up to that point means the days before it — not counting the day itself. You can't be part of the score you're trying to beat.
Which also settles the first day. Nothing came before it, so there's nothing for it to beat. It's skipped, always.
Let's do it by hand before we write anything. Five days: twelve pages, twenty, sixteen, thirty, eighteen.
Day zero. Skipped, as we said. The count stays at nothing.
Day one. What's behind it? Only day zero, twelve pages. And the average of a single number is just that number.
Twenty pages against an average of twelve. Beaten. That's one.
Day two. Two days behind us now: twelve and twenty.
Add them, thirty-two. Share that between two days, and the average is sixteen.
And that day you read sixteen. Exactly the average. Not a page more.
So did you beat it? No. Matching is not beating. That's the line most people get wrong, and the question does say more than, not as much as.
Day three. Three days behind: twelve, twenty and sixteen.
Forty-eight altogether, shared between three. Sixteen again.
Thirty pages against sixteen. Comfortably beaten. That's two.
Day four. Four days behind now, and they add up to seventy-eight.
Seventy-eight shared between four. Nineteen and a half — and notice the average has stopped being a whole number. That'll matter in a minute.
And eighteen pages doesn't reach it. So that's a no as well — but for a different reason from day two. That one tied. This one simply fell short.
So the answer is two. You solved it, and you haven't written a line of code.
Now look back at what your hand was actually doing, because that's the bit that turns into code.
You never once needed the whole list. At every step you only held two things: the total of the days behind you, and how many of them there were.
And the average isn't a third thing to carry. It falls out of those two whenever you want it — total, divided by how many.
That's the whole problem. Carry a total, carry a count, and the rest is arithmetic.
So here it is in code, a line at a time. Every one of them is something you already did with your hand.
The total of everything behind us. It starts at nothing, because at the start there is nothing behind us.
And the tally. Also nothing, for the same reason.
Then we walk the days from zero to the end. That i is the day we're standing on.
And this is the skip rule, written down. If i is zero we're on the first day, there's nothing behind us, and there's nothing to do.
Here's the average. And look what we divide by — i itself. How many days are behind you? Exactly your own day number. Day four has four behind it.

That word double is there because seventy-eight over four is nineteen and a half, and whole numbers can't hold a half. Divide one whole number by another and the fraction is simply thrown away — you'd get nineteen.

Here it happens not to change the answer, and it's worth knowing why: a whole number that beats the chopped average beats the real one too. But leaning on that is how you get bitten the day the question asks for the average itself.
Then the comparison. More than, strictly — the greater-than sign on its own, with no equals beside it. That single character is day two.
And only now, with the comparing done, do we add today's pages to the total.
Move that line one place up and the whole thing breaks quietly: you'd be measuring today against an average that already had today inside it.
And the closing bracket. Ten lines, and not one of them does anything you didn't do by hand.
So watch it go. I'll stop talking for this bit.
Two. The same answer your hand got, by exactly the same moves.
One last thing, and it's the sort of thing that separates an answer that works from a good one.
You could solve this without carrying a total at all. On every day, go back and add up all the days behind you from scratch.
Same answer, every time. But over a thousand days you'd be adding up half a million numbers instead of a thousand — and the question does allow a thousand days.
Carrying the total costs you one number of memory and saves you all of that. Which is usually what people mean when they say one solution is better than another.
